front.title: ChaCha20 and Poly1305: the quarter round

abstract.t: A fixture, not a specification: the quarter-round test vectors of RFC 8439 Sections 2.1.1 and 2.2.1, over a u32[] state, from spec to a run of the fixture quarter round in tests/fixtures/chacha20. Every binding sentence of RFC 8439 is quoted here, and those this fixture does not test are excluded.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

The module is the fixture quarter round of tests/fixtures/chacha20/fixture, run with --package fixture=tests/fixtures/chacha20/fixture. It takes the ChaCha state as 32-bit words and the indices of the four it operates on, and returns the state after the quarter round. Section 2.1.1 runs it on a state of four words, and Section 2.2.1 on the whole 16-word state.

front.title: ChaCha20 and Poly1305 for IETF Protocols

abstract.t: This document defines the ChaCha20 stream cipher as well as the use of the Poly1305 authenticator, both as stand-alone algorithms and as a "combined mode", or Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) algorithm.

RFC 7539, the predecessor of this document, was meant to serve as a stable reference and an implementation guide. It was a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG). This document merges the errata filed against RFC 7539 and adds a little text to the Security Considerations section.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.
